blocks.content: CrashLoopBackOff means a container keeps crashing and being restarted, and it exists specifically because of the restartPolicy: Always behavior covered in the Health Checks module.

A container crashes, kubelet restarts it (exactly the mechanism covered in the Restart Policies topic), it crashes again, and the cycle repeats, this status is Kubernetes's way of naming that exact repeating pattern.

blocks.alt: A real, repeating cycle, not a single, isolated crash

blocks.content: Each subsequent restart attempt waits longer than the last, an increasing backoff delay, this prevents a badly broken container from consuming resources in a tight, rapid restart loop, giving the system, and anyone investigating, some breathing room.

blocks.alt: A deliberately increasing delay, not an instant, rapid-fire restart loop

blocks.content: This is exactly the scenario the --previous flag, covered in the kubectl module's logs topic, exists for, the container's current logs are empty (it just restarted), --previous retrieves what it actually printed right before crashing.

blocks.alt: The exact scenario this flag exists for, the current logs alone are simply empty

blocks.content: The application logs almost always reveal the real cause, a missing required environment variable, a bad configuration value, or a genuine bug in application startup code are the most frequent culprits.

blocks.alt: The logs almost always reveal one of a handful of recurring, real causes

blocks.text: 5. Why This Loop Happens at All

blocks.content: This connects directly back to the Restart Policies topic, this entire cycle only happens because restartPolicy: Always keeps trying, exactly as designed, the fix is not disabling restarts, it is fixing whatever the logs reveal is actually wrong.

blocks.alt: The exact mechanism covered earlier, now seen from its failure-mode side

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: CrashLoopBackOff is a repeated crash-and-restart cycle with increasing delay, driven by the restartPolicy: Always mechanism covered in the Health Checks module.
kubectl logs --previous is the essential diagnostic tool here, since the container's current logs are always empty right after a fresh restart.
